Reference: Kang and Silveira (2021)

Model Setting

The paper quantifies the benefits of regulatory discretion in the enforcement of water pollution rules in California. Penalties for observably similar violations differ across dischargers (disparities in punishment), and two stories can explain this: regulators may differ in their own preferences (how much they care about pollution, how costly it is for them to punish), or they may use their expertise to tailor penalties to dischargers whose compliance costs differ. The paper builds a principal-agent model in the spirit of Becker (1968) and Mookherjee and Png (1994) in which a regulator sets a penalty schedule for each facility, and the facility, privately informed about its compliance cost, chooses an unobserved negligence level that stochastically generates violations. The model is nonparametrically identified by combining the facility first-order condition with an exogenous increase in enforcement stringency in 2006 (following d'Haultfoeuille and Fevrier 2020) and the regulator first-order condition (following Luo, Perrigne and Vuong 2018). The estimates show that most of the heterogeneity in penalties comes from heterogeneity in compliance costs, not in regulator preferences, and that removing discretion (a one-size-fits-all schedule or a linear schedule) raises penalties and enforcement costs while increasing violations by facilities whose violations the regulator views as most harmful.

Institutional Setting and Data

Discharges into surface waters are regulated through NPDES permits under the Clean Water Act and California's Porter-Cologne Act. Permittees submit self-monitoring reports; 95% of recorded violations in 2000-2014 were self-reported. Enforcement is carried out by nine Regional Water Quality Control Boards (seven part-time members appointed by the governor, relying on technical staff), overseen by the State Water Resources Control Board. The enforcement policy gives a penalty methodology (initial amount based on extent, severity and sensitivity of the receiving water, then adjustments for conduct, ability to pay, economic benefit, enforcement costs and environmental justice) but leaves wide room for discretion; the board's final penalty differs from the staff assessment in 24% of actions. Serious violations (exceeding limits for a group I pollutant by 40% or a group II pollutant by 20%) and chronic nonserious violations (four or more in six months) are subject to a mandatory minimum penalty (MMP) of 3,000 dollars per violation. Enforcement resources differ a lot across boards (from 109 to 539 permits per enforcement staff member).

The source of identifying variation is the 2006 institutional changes: the launch of the CIWQS electronic tracking and reporting system (July 2005) and the creation of a statewide Office of Enforcement (July 2006). Both lowered the administrative burden of enforcement. After the changes, average MMP violations per facility-quarter fell from 1.39 (2002-2005) to 1.10 (2009-2014), and the average penalty per violation within four years rose by about 1,300 dollars (95%), driven by the probability of a penalty (0.42 before, roughly doubling), not by the amount conditional on a penalty (3,280 versus 3,211 dollars). The sample is 228 domestic wastewater treatment facilities, responsible for 73% of effluent violations statewide. Descriptively, penalties conditional on violation attributes vary with facility and local attributes (major facilities, high-income counties and counties approving the 2006 water bond Proposition 84 are penalized more), the per-violation penalty increases with concurrent violations in the quarter (a concurrent violation raises the penalty probability by 9.3 percentage points), and past violations do not matter, which motivates a static, nonlinear penalty schedule.

Equilibrium

Pointwise optimization gives either a(θ)=0a(\theta)=0a(θ)=0 or the regulator's first-order condition:

h′[a(θ)]−b′[a(θ)]((1−ψ)θ+ψ[1−F(θ)]f(θ))=0(9.3.3.8)h'[a(\theta)]-b'[a(\theta)]\left((1-\psi)\theta+\frac{\psi[1-F(\theta)]}{f(\theta)}\right)=0 \tag{9.3.3.8}h′[a(θ)]−b′[a(θ)]((1−ψ)θ+f(θ)ψ[1−F(θ)]​)=0(9.3.3.8)

The bracket is a virtual type: it mixes the true marginal compliance cost θ\thetaθ with the information rent term [1−F(θ)]/f(θ)[1-F(\theta)]/f(\theta)[1−F(θ)]/f(θ), weighted by the enforcement cost ψ\psiψ. Under Assumption 2 ((i) the virtual type is positive and strictly increasing in θ\thetaθ; (ii) bbb strictly concave and hhh convex, or bbb concave and hhh strictly convex), Proposition 1 shows that the optimal schedule a∗(⋅)a^*(\cdot)a∗(⋅) is continuous and nondecreasing, characterized by this condition and strictly increasing where positive. The equilibrium is thus a menu: the regulator commits to e(⋅)e(\cdot)e(⋅) (equivalently ϵ(⋅)\epsilon(\cdot)ϵ(⋅)), each type self-selects its negligence via the facility first-order condition, and violations and penalties follow.

The equilibrium departs from the first best only when both frictions are present. With costless enforcement (ψ=0\psi=0ψ=0), the schedule e(a)=h(a)−h(0)e(a)=h(a)-h(0)e(a)=h(a)−h(0) makes the facility internalize the externality without the regulator knowing θ\thetaθ. With costly enforcement but observed types, a Pigouvian-like schedule achieves the first best with zero penalties paid in equilibrium:

e(a;θ)={0if a≤a∗∗(θ),θb′[a∗∗(θ)]{a−a∗∗(θ)}otherwise.(9.3.3.10)e(a;\theta)=\begin{cases}0 & \text{if } a\le a^{**}(\theta),\\ \theta b'[a^{**}(\theta)]\left\{a-a^{**}(\theta)\right\} & \text{otherwise.}\end{cases} \tag{9.3.3.10}e(a;θ)={0θb′[a∗∗(θ)]{a−a∗∗(θ)}​if a≤a∗∗(θ),otherwise.​(9.3.3.10)

With both private information and ψ>0\psi>0ψ>0, the regulator trades off deterrence against the enforcement cost of the penalties that are actually paid, which is why it is optimal to tailor schedules to each facility's type distribution and why optimal penalties are nonlinear.

The primitives for facility iii in period ttt are Fi,t(⋅)F_{i,t}(\cdot)Fi,t​(⋅), bi,t(⋅)b_{i,t}(\cdot)bi,t​(⋅), hi,t(⋅)h_{i,t}(\cdot)hi,t​(⋅) and ψi,t\psi_{i,t}ψi,t​, and all heterogeneity is captured by observables xi,t\mathbf{x}_{i,t}xi,t​: facility size, age, treatment technology, capacity utilization, water-board threat rating, watershed dissolved oxygen saturation, precipitation, and county irrigation use, income, density and Proposition 84 vote share, plus regional board dummies. Given e^j\hat{e}_je^j​ and G^j\hat{G}_jG^j​, the identification steps are applied separately at each xi,t\mathbf{x}_{i,t}xi,t​, with hhh restricted to be linear, hj(a∣xi,t)=γj(xi,t)ah_j(a|\mathbf{x}_{i,t})=\gamma_j(\mathbf{x}_{i,t})ahj​(a∣xi,t​)=γj​(xi,t​)a, so that each facility's perceived harm is one-dimensional. The outputs are F(⋅∣x)F(\cdot|\mathbf{x})F(⋅∣x), b′(⋅∣x)b'(\cdot|\mathbf{x})b′(⋅∣x), γpre(x)\gamma_{pre}(\mathbf{x})γpre​(x), γpost(x)\gamma_{post}(\mathbf{x})γpost​(x), ψpre(x)\psi_{pre}(\mathbf{x})ψpre​(x) and ψpost(x)\psi_{post}(\mathbf{x})ψpost​(x), computed for the 221 facilities active in the first quarter of 2005, with bootstrap inference.

Key Estimates

  • Fit: the model matches the share of facility-quarters with zero violations (data 0.771 versus model 0.789 before, 0.843 versus 0.805 after) and the average quarterly penalty (2,381 versus 2,318 dollars before; 2,215 versus 2,119 after). The estimated penalty schedule is strictly convex in the number of violations.

  • Compliance costs: the median marginal compliance cost θb^′(a∣x)\theta\hat{b}'(a|\mathbf{x})θb^′(a∣x) (at the median type and a low pre-2006 negligence level) is 1,431.0 dollars, with an interquartile range of 1,084.4.

  • Perceived harm γ\gammaγ: median 3,589.4 before and 3,157.1 after 2006; the change (−114.5-114.5−114.5) is insignificant.

  • Enforcement cost ψ\psiψ: median 0.865 dollars per dollar of penalty before and 0.204 after; the median change is −0.551-0.551−0.551 (95% interval [−0.745,−0.239][-0.745,-0.239][−0.745,−0.239]). The stringency increase is therefore rationalized by a fall in enforcement costs, consistent with the purpose of CIWQS and the Office of Enforcement.

  • Regulator vs. local preferences: in regressions of log estimates on attributes, γpre\gamma_{pre}γpre​ is about 47% higher and ψpre\psi_{pre}ψpre​ about 29% lower for facilities in high-income counties (above 57,000 dollars), and ψpre\psi_{pre}ψpre​ is about 13% lower where Proposition 84 won a majority, suggesting that regulators reflect local demand for water quality.

  • Disparities: expected penalties at the average pre-2006 negligence (a=1.08a=1.08a=1.08) correlate positively with the regulator's marginal benefit of compliance,

    γpre(xi,t)+ψpre(xi,t)e′(a∣xi,t)(9.3.3.20)\gamma_{pre}(\mathbf{x}_{i,t})+\psi_{pre}(\mathbf{x}_{i,t})e'(a|\mathbf{x}_{i,t}) \tag{9.3.3.20}γpre​(xi,t​)+ψpre​(xi,t​)e′(a∣xi,t​)(9.3.3.20)

    but much of the variation is explained by compliance costs: it is optimal to punish more where marginal compliance costs are higher, so a facility with low perceived harm may still face stringent penalties.

Counterfactuals

All results use pre-2006 estimates and are proportional changes relative to the baseline.

  • Median regulator (all facilities face the median γ\gammaγ and ψ\psiψ, but schedules remain tailored): the standard deviation of expected penalties at a=1.08a=1.08a=1.08 falls by only 11% (insignificant); mean violations +5.5%+5.5\%+5.5%, mean penalties −11.9%-11.9\%−11.9%. Heterogeneity in regulator preferences is not the main driver of disparities; heterogeneity in compliance costs is.

  • One-size-fits-all policy: the regulator chooses a single schedule (a cubic in kkk for k≥1k\ge1k≥1, zero for no violations) to minimize the sum of expected costs across all facilities,

    min⁡e(⋅)∑i∫0θˉ(hi[ai(θ)]+ψie[ai(θ)]+θ{bi(aˉ)−bi[ai(θ)]})fi(θ) dθ(9.3.3.21)\min_{e(\cdot)}\sum_i\int_0^{\bar{\theta}}\Big(h_i[a_i(\theta)]+\psi_ie[a_i(\theta)]+\theta\left\{b_i(\bar{a})-b_i[a_i(\theta)]\right\}\Big)f_i(\theta)\,d\theta \tag{9.3.3.21}e(⋅)min​i∑​∫0θˉ​(hi​[ai​(θ)]+ψi​e[ai​(θ)]+θ{bi​(aˉ)−bi​[ai​(θ)]})fi​(θ)dθ(9.3.3.21)

    where ai(θ)a_i(\theta)ai​(θ) is facility iii's best response. Mean violations fall by 6.1% but total penalties rise by 1.3%; a simple set of tailored schedules achieving the same 6% reduction would lower penalties by 2.5% relative to the uniform policy. Violations increase at major facilities, high-threat facilities, and facilities in high-income and high-approval counties, precisely those the regulator perceives as having high benefits of compliance.

  • Linear penalties: schedules must satisfy

    ϵ(k∣x)=p(x)k⟹e(a∣x)=p(x)a(9.3.3.22)\epsilon(k|\mathbf{x})=p(\mathbf{x})k\quad\Longrightarrow\quad e(a|\mathbf{x})=p(\mathbf{x})a \tag{9.3.3.22}ϵ(k∣x)=p(x)k⟹e(a∣x)=p(x)a(9.3.3.22)

    Convex penalties let the regulator punish high-θ\thetaθ draws (many violations) heavily while keeping penalties low for occasional violators. Under linearity, violations fall by 5.9% but penalties rise by 15.8%; a linear penalty that reproduces each facility's baseline expected violations would raise penalties by 10%.

  • No enforcement costs (ψ=0\psi=0ψ=0, first best): violations fall by 23% and penalties rise by 48.5%; compliance costs rise by 35%, external costs fall by 25% and enforcement costs rise by 55%. On average, marginal penalties are below marginal harm, as in Mookherjee and Png (1994) for mild offenses.

  • Green regulator: every facility faces γ=max⁡{γ^pre(xi,t)}=8,020\gamma=\max\{\hat{\gamma}_{pre}(\mathbf{x}_{i,t})\}=8{,}020γ=max{γ^​pre​(xi,t​)}=8,020 and ψ=0.015\psi=0.015ψ=0.015 (observed staff cost per dollar of penalty). Violations fall by 51% and penalties rise by 77%, an upper bound on violations that could be attributed to private interests (corruption or lack of dedication) of regulators.

Overall, discretion lets regulators use their expertise on compliance costs to economize on costly enforcement and to reflect local preferences, so restricting it is costly unless regulator preferences are badly misaligned.

So the marginal expected penalty is the expected penalty increment from one more violation. This is the objective of a facility of type θ\thetaθ that chooses negligence aaa. The first term is minus the compliance cost: full negligence aˉ\bar{a}aˉ is the costless benchmark, and bringing negligence down to aaa costs θ[b(aˉ)−b(a)]≥0\theta[b(\bar{a})-b(a)]\ge 0θ[b(aˉ)−b(a)]≥0 dollars per quarter, because b(⋅)b(\cdot)b(⋅) is increasing. The second term is the expected penalty from equation (1). Both terms are in dollars, and the payoff is nonpositive.

The multiplicative form θb(a)\theta b(a)θb(a) is what makes the model tractable. This is the regulator's objective for one facility: an expected cost, averaged over the type distribution f(θ)f(\theta)f(θ) because the regulator does not observe θ\thetaθ. For each type the integrand has three components, all in dollars per quarter. First, h[a(θ)]h[a(\theta)]h[a(θ)] is the environmental cost of the facility's negligence as perceived by the regulator. Second, ψe[a(θ)]\psi e[a(\theta)]ψe[a(θ)] is the enforcement cost: the penalty itself is a transfer from the facility to the state and does not enter, but each dollar collected costs the regulator ψ\psiψ dollars of administrative and political effort. The regulator takes into account that a(θ)a(\theta)a(θ) is the facility's best response to the schedule, equation (3). If hhh were true harm and ψ\psiψ the true resource cost of enforcement, this would be utilitarian social cost, as in Becker and in Mookherjee and Png. The paper instead treats hhh and ψ\psiψ as the regulator's preferences, to be recovered from behavior. Two features matter later. Because the weight on compliance costs is fixed at one, the levels of hhh and ψ\psiψ are identified relative to dollars of compliance cost. And because ψ>0\psi>0ψ>0, the regulator dislikes penalties that are actually paid; this is the force that, together with private information, moves the solution away from the first best of equation (9). Substituting the implementability formula (6) turns this objective into equation (7), and the same objective summed over facilities defines the one-size-fits-all counterfactual in equation (21).

This is the parametric restriction on the regulator's perceived environmental cost used in the third identification step. This is a sample-selection (type II Tobit) model of the penalty that facility iii receives in quarter ttt, as a function of its number of violations ki,tk_{i,t}ki,t​. The first line is a latent index for whether any penalty is imposed: it is linear in the attributes xi,t\mathbf{x}_{i,t}xi,t​, in a post-reform dummy and in ki,tk_{i,t}ki,t​, with a unit-variance normal error, so it is a probit. The second line is the latent amount: its median is exp⁡(xi,tϕ2,x)ki,t+ϕ2,k2ki,t2\exp(\mathbf{x}_{i,t}\phi_{2,x})k_{i,t}+\phi_{2,k^2}k_{i,t}^2exp(xi,t​ϕ2,x​)ki,t​+ϕ2,k2​ki,t2​, a per-violation rate that depends on attributes plus a quadratic term, with a multiplicative lognormal error. The third line says that the amount is observed only when the index is nonnegative; otherwise the penalty is zero.

The form matches the institutional facts: many violations subject to the mandatory minimum penalty go unpenalized, so there is a mass at zero; the amount is positive and skewed, hence the logarithm; and ϕ2,k2>0\phi_{2,k^2}>0ϕ2,k2​>0 produces the convexity in kkk seen in the data. The amount is zero at k=0k=0k=0. The covariance σ12\sigma_{12}σ12​ lets unobserved features such as severity move both the chance and the size of a penalty. The reform enters only through ϕ1,post\phi_{1,post}ϕ1,post​, in line with the finding that the probability of a penalty rose while the conditional amount did not.

This is the empirical counterpart of the definition in equation (1). The penalty for kkk violations is replaced by the fitted Tobit mean from equation (17), evaluated at the maximum likelihood estimate ϕ^\hat{\phi}ϕ^​, and the infinite Poisson sum is cut off at k=150k=150k=150. The result is a smooth function of the negligence level aaa for each regime jjj and each attribute vector xi,t\mathbf{x}_{i,t}xi,t​, measured in dollars per quarter. The term k=0k=0k=0 contributes nothing, because the fitted schedule is zero when there are no violations.

The truncation is harmless in practice. The neglected tail is weighted by Poisson probabilities of more than 150 violations, and the relevant negligence levels are of the order of one violation per quarter (the pre-2006 mean is 1.08), so these probabilities are numerically zero even though the fitted penalty grows quadratically in kkk. Note that the Tobit is estimated on quarters with at most 25 violations, so for larger kkk the schedule is an extrapolation of the parametric form; this matters little for the same reason.

What the later steps need is the derivative of this schedule, which enters the vertical transform in equation (12), the identification of b′b'b′ in equation (14) and the marginal benefit in equation (20). Differentiating term by term as for equation (1),

Two facilities with the same γ\gammaγ and ψ\psiψ can therefore face very different marginal penalties e′(a)=θb′(a)e'(a)=\theta b'(a)e′(a)=θb′(a) when their cost primitives b′b'b′ and FFF differ, which is the paper's explanation of disparities. This is the regulator's problem when discretion is removed and one schedule must apply to every facility. The integrand is the same per-facility expected cost as in equation (4), now with facility-specific primitives: perceived harm hih_ihi​, enforcement cost ψi\psi_iψi​, baseline compliance cost bib_ibi​ and type density fif_ifi​, all taken from the pre-2006 estimates. In the baseline each facility has its own schedule eie_iei​ that solves equation (8) for its own (Fi,bi,hi,ψi)(F_i,b_i,h_i,\psi_i)(Fi​,bi​,hi​,ψi​). Here the same marginal penalty faces all facilities, so the pointwise condition (8) cannot hold facility by facility; the optimal uniform schedule only balances the marginal costs on average. The constraint therefore weakly raises the objective. The comparison with the baseline measures the value of tailoring penalties to the regulator's knowledge of compliance costs and to heterogeneous preferences.

A simple way to see the loss: if harm is linear and enforcement is costless, a common schedule gives any two facilities that choose the same negligence level the same marginal penalty e′(a)e'(a)e′(a), while the first best in equation (9) requires a marginal penalty e′=γie'=\gamma_ie′=γi​ specific to each facility. Facilities with γi\gamma_iγi​ above the common slope are under-deterred and those below are over-deterred. This is the pattern in the results: violations rise at facilities with high perceived benefits of compliance, even though average violations fall by 6.1 percent and total penalties rise by 1.3 percent.

which is well defined when bbb is strictly concave. The regulator is left with a single instrument per facility, the slope p(x)p(\mathbf{x})p(x), so all types face the same marginal penalty and the type-by-type condition (8) cannot be met. The expected penalty paid by type θ\thetaθ is p(x)a(θ)p(\mathbf{x})a(\theta)p(x)a(θ), which is positive even at low negligence levels, whereas a convex schedule keeps penalties low for occasional violators and steep for frequent ones. This explains why the linear counterfactual raises penalties collected, and hence enforcement costs, by 15.8 percent while violations fall by 5.9 percent.
